conflicts_flagged.conflict: The operator asked for a review of views, engagement and follows on the published posts.
conflicts_flagged.resolved: Impossible and reported as such at the top of the handover. There is no Instagram access — no handle, no credential — so no figure exists to review. Fabricating an analysis would be the single most damaging thing this system could do, because every future decision would be built on it. Asked instead for either the credential or a screenshot of Insights.

conflicts_flagged.conflict: Asked for average money-lost figures for Melbourne salons and barbers due to poor booking systems.
conflicts_flagged.resolved: No such figure exists in citable form. Every salon no-show number findable online comes from a company selling booking software (Etisia, Boulevard, Bookeo, Bella Booking, Lutily); they disagree with each other across 5-15%, 14%, 15% and 23%; none is Melbourne-specific; none traces to a primary source. Kairo is itself a booking vendor, so repeating a rival vendor's self-serving number is the fastest way to lose a reader who checks. Built the educational posts on the one figure that could be verified by reading the page — IBISWorld's Australian market size — plus arithmetic the reader completes with their own numbers, and said out loud in the caption why no percentage is quoted. On an account selling booking software, refusing to cite a booking-vendor statistic is itself the credibility play.

research_findings.finding: The screenshots really were soft, and it was measurable: every product frame shipped between 1.5x and 2.7x upsampled.
research_findings.source: Direct measurement of shipped crops against the 1240x775 source frames.
research_findings.consequence: Two causes. Cards rendered at deviceScaleFactor 2, exporting a 1080 canvas at 2160px when Instagram serves at 1080 — doubling the stretch for nothing. And crops cut tight then displayed wide. Fixed both: everything now renders at native delivery size, and tools/media.mjs audits every crop's magnification and flags anything over 1.35x. This week's frames are 0.97x-1.30x.

research_findings.finding: Reel craft: the decision to keep watching happens in about a second; a slow build-up is the most common way to lose it; curiosity-gap and pattern-interrupt openings outperform bold claims; one idea per reel beats a tour.
research_findings.source: Aggregated secondary sources, 2026-09-06. The technique is well established and consistent across sources; the engagement percentages quoted alongside it do not resolve to primary sources.
research_findings.consequence: Technique applied to all three reels — problem on screen inside one second, no title cards. None of the percentages are quoted anywhere in the pack.

research_findings.finding: Cinematic vocabulary that works on static UI: dolly push-in, parallax, rack focus, whip pan with motion blur, light sweep, letterbox, kinetic type stagger.
research_findings.consequence: Built into tools/reel-lib.mjs as transition kinds, driven by a real cubic-bezier solver on the site's own curve so the video moves like the website.

research_findings.finding: Australian Hairdressing & Beauty Services was $12.5bn in 2026, down 0.9% that year, having grown at a 1.8% CAGR since 2021.
research_findings.consequence: The only third-party figure used in three weeks of packs. Read off the page rather than off a search summary, cited on the slide itself, and declared in verified_figures. It is national, not Melbourne, and the copy says Australia. It also carries the strategic point: a flat market means the win is in keeping clients rather than adding them, which is exactly what a booking system affects.

research_findings.finding: No credible salon no-show statistic exists for Australia or Melbourne.
research_findings.source: Searched 2026-09-06; every result was a booking-software vendor's blog.
research_findings.consequence: Recorded in CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md so the next run does not go looking again, and so the substitute move (reader-completed arithmetic, stated transparently) is reusable.
